LEARNING PATH LESSON · FEELINGS & KINDNESS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Be Kind, Helpful, Patient & Honest — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson turns four big values into four small jobs — because at four, character is not discussed, it is DISPATCHED: one kindness mission, one helper job, one waiting moment, one honest report.

What is this?

Be kind, be helpful, be patient and be honest are the be-words: kindness done on purpose, help spotted and given, patience practised in real queues, honesty told in real wobbly moments.

What does it mean?

"Be" words work differently from other words — they name the child, not just the act. A child who hears "you were patient today" starts collecting evidence of being a patient person, and identity drives behaviour far more than rules do.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ideas: be-words are JOBS, not grades (small, today-sized, doable); helpful means SEEING the job (eyes first, hands second); and honest earns more than it costs — the true answer is always received warmly in this house.

Why this matters

This card sits after the feelings vocabulary because character needs a base: children who can name feelings find it far easier to be kind, patient and honest — the be-words are where the vocabulary becomes visible.

What it teaches

Prosocial identity formation, helping behaviour (initiated, not assigned), delay of gratification in natural settings, and moral courage — the honest report is a four-year-old’s first ethics exam.

Words to learn

be kindhelpfulpatienthonestmissionjobtrue

Say this to your child

“"Here are the four be-words, and each one is a job for today. Be kind — one kindness mission, your choice: a drawing delivered, a sibling helped, a flower found. Be helpful — eyes open for a job nobody asked you to do; helping first is the whole trick. Be patient — one waiting moment, felt on purpose: hands quiet, breath slow, timer ticking. Be honest — when the question comes, tell it true, even the wobbly parts; in this family, true answers are always safe. Do the four jobs and something funny happens: they stop being jobs. They start being you."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Four be-words — each one a job you can do today."
  2. Read the panels: heart-shaped hands BE KIND, the teddy packed into a box BE HELPFUL, folded hands BE PATIENT, the hand-on-chest girl BE HONEST.
  3. Dispatch the missions: one kindness mission (child’s choice), one helper job (socks match, cushions returned), one waiting moment (the oven timer), one honest moment (a question answered true).
  4. Debrief each with the word, not the lecture: "you WERE patient. You WERE honest."
  5. Close with the takeaway: "be-words are not rules — they are costumes you can try on, and they start to fit."

Look closer at the picture

On this card four panels give the be-words bodies: Be Kind, a boy shaping a heart with his hands; Be Helpful, a girl tucking a teddy bear into a box; Be Patient, a boy with folded hands and closed eyes; and Be Honest, a girl with a hand on her chest — values drawn as actions, not posters.

Ask your child

"What is your kindness mission today?" "How do we spot a job nobody asked for?" "What does the patient body do?" "Is the true answer always safe here?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "I WAS patient!" "I helped without being asked" or the brave one: "it was me who knocked it over."

Out in the real world

The be-words have job sites everywhere: the neighbours’ bins (helpful), the waiting room (patient), the who-drew-on-the-wall tribunal (honest), the sibling’s fallen tower (kind). Dispatch small and often — four tiny jobs a day build more character than any poster on the wall.

Try it together

Mission Control: each morning, pick ONE be-word as the day’s secret mission and write it where the child can see. At dinner, the family reports mission evidence — and everyone hunts for the mission in EACH OTHER. A week later, the child picks the missions for the grown-ups. Watching a four-year-old assign "be patient" to a parent is character education at its finest.

Understanding check

Ask: "Which be-word spots jobs nobody asked for? Which one tells it true? What do be-words become after enough practice?" Helpful, honest, you — three answers and the be-words are on the job.

Parent tips

Praise in the past tense of identity — "you were so patient waiting for the glue" — not "good boy": the first builds a self-image, the second builds a compliance habit. And when the honest report is hard to hear, thank the honesty before addressing the mess; the order of those two sentences decides whether honesty survives to age five.

This lesson pairs with the Be Kind, Helpful, Patient & Honest flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Feelings & Kindness (Class 38).
